## Research question

Does the latest New York Times Hardcover Fiction best-seller list contain more recent arrivals or more books that have stayed on the list for several weeks? How does this compare with the list from 52 weeks earlier?

## API and request

I will use the NYT Books API in R. This endpoint returns a best-seller list for a selected date:

`GET https://api.nytimes.com/svc/books/v3/lists/{date}/hardcover-fiction.json`

The first request uses `current` as the date. For the second request, I subtract 364 days from the publication date returned in the first response. This keeps the weekday the same, although it may differ from the exact calendar date a year earlier.

The list is `hardcover-fiction`, and the `api-key` query parameter reads the key from the `NYT_API_KEY` environment variable. The key stays in a private `.Renviron` file and is not included in the report or on GitHub.

## Working with the data

I will use `httr::GET()` to request the data and check the response status. I will save the JSON responses in a `data` folder so the report can reuse the same lists without making new requests.

I will read the responses with `jsonlite::fromJSON()` and convert `results$books` into a tibble. Each row will represent one book on one dated list.

The table will include rank, previous rank, weeks on the list, title, author, publisher, description, primary ISBN, and the list publication date. I will remove extra spaces, replace empty strings with `NA`, and keep ISBNs as text. Nested fields such as additional ISBNs and purchase links are not needed for this comparison. I will also check for empty lists, duplicate ranks, and missing or negative week counts.

## Comparing the lists

For each week, I will calculate the median weeks on the list and count books in two groups:

- Recent arrivals: two weeks or fewer.
- Long-running entries: ten weeks or more.

Books with three to nine weeks will fall between these groups. These definitions describe time on the list, not the age of a book.

I will show the five highest-ranked books, compare the longest-running entries, and make a bar chart of weeks on the list. The conclusion will state which group is larger, whether it forms a majority, and whether the two weeks differ.

## Limits

Two lists can show a difference between weeks, but they cannot establish a trend. The results apply only to Hardcover Fiction, and weeks on the list do not measure the number of copies sold.
